strengths: Identifies and clearly formalizes two widespread yet underexplored failure modes in prompt optimization and LLM memory systems: brevity bias and context collapse.

The proposed architecture (Generator, Reflector, Curator with structured delta updates and grow-and-refine pruning) is principled, modular, and directly prevents context collapse while maintaining comprehensive domain-specific playbooks.

Compelling experimental results across offline and online settings on difficult, realistic benchmarks (AppWorld, FiNER, Formula), demonstrating large improvements (+10.6% on agents, +8.6% on finance) over strong baselines like GEPA, MIPROv2, and Dynamic Cheatsheet.
Impressive efficiency advantages: incremental updates avoid repetitive full-context regeneration, leading to over 80% reduction in adaptation latency and rollout/token costs.

Fair experimental methodology: isolates the effect of context engineering by using the identical model (DeepSeek-V3.1) for all three roles, preventing hidden knowledge distillation from stronger models.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is focused primarily on AppWorld and financial datasets; including additional agent or reasoning benchmarks (e.g., SWE-bench, WebArena, or complex mathematical reasoning) would further substantiate the general applicability across diverse agentic workflows.

While Section 5 insightfully discusses that long contexts do not necessarily incur high serving costs due to KV cache reuse, the paper lacks explicit empirical measurements of inference-time latency, KV cache memory footprint, and time-to-first-token (TTFT) under realistic deployment settings.

The grow-and-refine mechanism relies on semantic embeddings and similarity thresholds for deduplication and counter tracking, but the paper provides limited ablation or sensitivity analysis regarding threshold selection and memory growth bounds over extremely long horizons.

strengths: Identifies and clearly formalizes a significant practical failure mode in iterative prompt/context optimization: 'context collapse' (where end-to-end LLM rewriting abruptly compresses and discards vital task knowledge) and 'brevity bias'.

Presents a clean, modular, and systems-oriented solution (ACE) combining a Generator-Reflector-Curator division of labor with itemized delta updates and deterministic deduplication, avoiding costly and unstable monolithic prompt rewrites.

Strong empirical performance across both offline (system prompt optimization) and online (test-time memory) settings. On the challenging AppWorld benchmark, ACE enables an open-source model (DeepSeek-V3.1) to achieve performance comparable to production agents using GPT-4.1.
Demonstrates substantial efficiency gains in both token cost and adaptation latency (over 75% fewer rollouts than GEPA; over 80% cost reduction compared to Dynamic Cheatsheet).
Detailed appendix including full prompt templates and ablation studies analyzing the contributions of the Reflector, multi-epoch refinement, and offline warmup.
weaknesses: Incremental conceptual novelty: The core framework builds directly on prior memory and reflection frameworks such as Dynamic Cheatsheet and A-MEM; the primary contribution lies in system engineering (delta updates, ID tracking, and semantic deduplication) rather than fundamentally new learning principles.

Strong dependence on feedback quality: Performance drops noticeably on tasks lacking definitive execution signals or ground truth supervision (e.g., FiNER online adaptation drops below the base LLM without ground-truth feedback), highlighting limits to unsupervised test-time adaptation.

Ambiguity regarding context scaling and retrieval: Section 3.1 states that itemized bullets enable 'fine-grained retrieval', but the Generator prompts in Appendix D appear to insert the entire playbook (`{{ playbook }}`) into the context window. It is unclear whether and how vector/BM25 retrieval was used during evaluation or if full context stuffing was employed.

Task scope is somewhat narrow: The evaluation is concentrated on AppWorld and two financial XBRL benchmarks. Including additional domains (e.g., SWE-bench, WebArena, or standard multi-step mathematical reasoning) would strengthen the generality of the conclusions.

strengths: Clearly identifies and articulates two key failure modes in iterative context optimization: brevity bias (over-abstraction omitting domain heuristics) and context collapse (information loss caused by monolithic rewriting).

The proposed ACE framework introduces a practical and modular design (Generator, Reflector, Curator) with structured delta updates and grow-and-refine deduplication, directly resolving context collapse without requiring full context regeneration.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across both offline prompt optimization and online test-time memory adaptation, demonstrating solid gains (+10.6% on AppWorld, +8.6% on financial benchmarks) over strong baselines including GEPA, MIPROv2, and Dynamic Cheatsheet.
Significant efficiency improvements over existing methods, achieving over 80% reduction in adaptation latency and rollout cost due to localized delta edits rather than costly global rewrites.
Good reproducibility and research transparency, including explicit failure analysis in low-feedback settings and detailed system prompts in the appendix.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental, as the tripartite architecture heavily builds upon prior agentic memory frameworks such as Dynamic Cheatsheet, Reflexion, and A-MEM.

Evaluation domain breadth is relatively narrow, focusing only on the AppWorld agent benchmark and two financial XBRL datasets (FiNER and Formula); testing on broader agent benchmarks (e.g., SWE-bench, WebArena) or general reasoning tasks would strengthen generalizability claims.

Strong vulnerability to noisy or absent execution feedback: as shown in Table 2 (FiNER online without GT labels drops by -3.4%), the framework risks accumulating spurious context items when clear environmental verification signals are missing.

Key implementation details regarding the grow-and-refine mechanism are underspecified in Section 3.2, such as the exact embedding model used for semantic deduplication, similarity thresholds, and pruning criteria.

strengths: The paper clearly diagnoses two fundamental failure modes in existing prompt and context optimization frameworks: brevity bias (over-compressing into generic instructions) and context collapse (destructive loss of accumulated knowledge during monolithic LLM rewrites).

The proposed ACE framework is well-principled, introducing a clean modular separation of concerns (Generator, Reflector, Curator) combined with incremental delta updates and grow-and-refine logic that prevents context collapse.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning both interactive multi-turn agent benchmarks (AppWorld) and domain-specific knowledge-intensive tasks (FiNER, Formula, DDXPlus, BIRD-SQL) under both offline and online adaptation settings.

Strong empirical gains over well-established baselines including GEPA, Dynamic Cheatsheet, MIPROv2, and standard ICL, matching or exceeding strong closed-source systems on AppWorld while using open-source models.

Detailed system and cost analysis showing that incremental updates substantially decrease adaptation latency and token rollouts compared to iterative full-prompt optimizers, supported by a realistic discussion of KV-cache amortization.
Extensive ablations and robustness checks, including model family generalization (DeepSeek-V3.1, GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-5.1, Llama-3.3-70B), reflector quality degradation, and hyperparameter sensitivity.
weaknesses: Performance remains sensitive to the presence of reliable feedback signals; as shown in the online experiments without ground-truth labels on FiNER, performance can degrade below the base model when neither ground truth nor programmatic execution feedback (e.g., unit tests or REPL errors) is present.

The grow-and-refine mechanism relies on relatively simple embedding-based deduplication and length-based pruning thresholds, which may struggle with complex cross-bullet contradictions or subtle semantic shifts over long operating horizons.

In continuous online adaptation, frequent updates to the context playbook will invalidate KV cache prefixes unless specialized modular caching or chunked prefix-sharing systems are used, which slightly complicates the serving efficiency claims during rapid online adaptation.

strengths: Identifies and systematically articulates two critical failure modes in iterative context/prompt optimization: brevity bias (over-abstracting domain rules into generic instructions) and context collapse (abrupt information loss from monolithic LLM rewrites).

Presents a well-structured and modular architecture dividing responsibilities between Generator, Reflector, and Curator, combined with deterministic, incremental delta updates that prevent context erosion.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning multi-turn interactive agents (AppWorld) and specialized domain tasks (FiNER, Formula, DDXPlus, BIRD-SQL) across both offline and online test-time adaptation.

Demonstrates substantial efficiency and latency improvements over strong baselines (e.g., >80% reduction in adaptation latency compared to GEPA and Dynamic Cheatsheet), supported by a thorough cost breakdown and KV cache reuse analysis.

Extensive analysis of generalization across multiple model families (DeepSeek-V3.1, Llama-3.3-70B, GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-5.1) and robust ablation/stress tests, including resilience against noisy or adversarial reflection feedback.
weaknesses: The grow-and-refine mechanism in Section 3.2 is described relatively briefly; inclusion of a formal algorithm or pseudocode detailing the exact metadata scoring, counter updates, and semantic deduplication rules in the main text would improve clarity.

In unsupervised online adaptation settings without reliable environment signals (e.g., on FiNER without ground truth), performance degrades due to noise accumulation, indicating a continued vulnerability to spurious feedback when verifiable execution signals are unavailable.

While KV cache reuse mitigates token generation costs, accumulating very long contexts (up to tens of thousands of tokens) can still increase memory footprint and time-to-first-token latency in high-concurrency serving environments where session cache hits are not guaranteed.

strengths: Identifies and convincingly illustrates two critical failure modes in existing context adaptation and prompt optimization methods: 'brevity bias' (loss of domain-specific heuristics to overly concise summaries) and 'context collapse' (abrupt degradation during monolithic context rewriting).

Well-motivated modular design that decomposes context engineering into Generator, Reflector, and Curator roles, utilizing itemized bullet-based delta updates rather than destructive end-to-end rewrites.

Extensive and rigorous experimental evaluation spanning diverse tasks (multi-turn interactive coding agent AppWorld, financial information extraction and numerical reasoning, medical diagnostic reasoning, and Text-to-SQL).

Demonstrates strong performance across both offline optimization and online test-time continuous adaptation, operating effectively even without ground-truth labels by exploiting natural execution feedback in agent environments.

Detailed efficiency and cost analysis demonstrating significant reductions in adaptation latency (-82% to -91%) and rollout requirements compared to prior baselines like GEPA and Dynamic Cheatsheet, supplemented by a practical analysis of KV cache reuse during inference.

Comprehensive ablation and robustness studies exploring incremental updates vs. monolithic rewrites, reflection depth, sensitivity to deduplication and pruning thresholds, weak reflector models, and resilience to noisy/adversarial reflections.
weaknesses: Dependence on reliable feedback signals: In pure domain-specific classification/tagging tasks (e.g., FiNER) lacking ground-truth supervision or verifiable environment signals (such as unit test results or execution errors), online adaptation can lead to playbook pollution and slight performance degradation.

Scalability to massive multi-domain playbooks: Although the 'grow-and-refine' mechanism incorporates deduplication and context pruning up to 100K tokens, the method currently places the consolidated playbook directly into the prompt rather than benchmarking dynamic sub-index retrieval mechanisms for scaling to very large suites of heterogenous tasks.

The core components (reflective prompting, JSON schema curation, embedding-based deduplication, and utility counters) represent an agentic systems integration and workflow refinement over frameworks like Dynamic Cheatsheet rather than a fundamentally new learning paradigm, though their empirical efficacy is undeniable.
